intro:
In three sittings, you build one working program: a ledger, the bank's book of accounts and of every movement of money between them. Many threads move money at once, and not one cent may be lost or created. By the end, the ledger never deadlocks, closes without dropping a transfer it accepted, shows balances that always add up, and serves 10,000 customers at once on virtual threads, while a slow outside safety service sits behind a shared limit and a deadline. Then you defend the design in a review, and you can name the earlier lesson behind each line of it.

The capstone draws on all of Part 1, and calls back its pictures as it goes. Lesson 1 uses the bank's races, the vault key, Ana and Ben's frozen transfers and the stress test from Threads and the bugs they cause, and the sealed envelope from The Java Memory Model. Lesson 2 uses the kitchen with its cooks and order rail, Little's law and closing time from Thread pools and executors, and the cashier's key and the OPEN/CLOSED sign from the memory model. Lesson 3 uses the order slips, the grill tokens and the hot pan from Virtual threads. There is little new theory. Each section shows what breaks if you choose differently, then names the lesson that explains why.

The lab lives in `labs/ledger`, one package per lesson (`workbench.ledger.l01` to `l03`). Each lesson's starter code contains the previous lesson's solution, so you can start any sitting fresh. Lessons 1 and 2 are in Java; lesson 3 adds a Kotlin server on top of the same Java ledger, the way a Kotlin program calls a Java library. From `labs/`, run `./gradlew :ledger:test --tests 'workbench.ledger.lNN.*'` until it passes; `solutionTest` runs the same tests against the reference answers. The tests check what a real bank cares about (the rules under 8 threads, no lost transfer at shutdown, a limit that holds at 10,000 requests), never timings. The Try-it demos run with `./gradlew :ledger:demo -Pmain=...`, and two of them get stuck on purpose so you can read a thread dump. Install JDK 25, and keep `jcmd` (it comes with the JDK) and `jq` (a small, free tool for reading JSON) at hand.
recap: Start from the rules: money is conserved, no balance goes below zero, a transfer is whole or not at all. Every lock and every happens-before rule in the program protects one of them.
One `ReentrantLock` per account, taken in one global id order, lets transfers on different accounts overlap without deadlock; the balance check lives inside the same critical section as the move.
A transfer is a value that can't change, checked when it's built, so any thread sees it whole; a reused, changeable row handed to a pool delivers the wrong data.
Stress tests make threads collide behind a start latch and check every rule, at the end and where it can break. A pass is evidence, not proof.
The ledger pool is sized by Little's law (8 threads, 80 slots), bounded and named, and it turns overflow away by counting and throwing: a visible "busy, try again", never a lost transfer.
Shutdown drains within a deadline, then cancels and hands back what never started. The journal is written before `apply`, so an interrupt never leaves half a transfer.
A whole snapshot holds every account lock in order, copies, and publishes a record that never changes through one volatile field; readers never lock.

Requests run on one new virtual thread each, behind written-down limits: a shared semaphore for the safety service, the bounded ledger pool, and one deadline per request with the small-amount rule as its fallback.
Fail-fast screening takes answers in the order they finish and ends with `shutdownNow()` and `close()`, so no call outlives its request or keeps a permit.
Thread dumps find what tests can't: a pool parked on its own futures in `Thread.print -l`, and 10,000 virtual threads grouped by container and stack in the JSON dump.

quiz.q: Two transfers run at once: acc-07 to acc-03, and acc-03 to acc-07. With the ledger's lock order, which lock does each take first?
options: Each takes its `from` account first
Both take acc-03 first
Both take acc-07 first
Whichever thread starts first decides
quiz.why: The order is by id, whichever way the money moves, so both lock acc-03 first. The second thread waits while holding nothing: a short wait, not a deadlock. "`from` first" is the order that freezes, the way Ana and Ben's transfers did.

quiz.q: A stress test of a ledger that checks the balance before taking the locks reports a total of 500,000 and no negative balances at the end. Why did it miss the bug?
options: Accounts went below zero during the run, and later credits topped them up before the final check
The race can't happen on Intel and AMD processors
The JIT removed the check
Eight threads are too few to cause a race
quiz.why: Each move was still one step under both locks, so the total held, and the overdrafts healed before the end. Check a rule where it can break as well: `debit` refusing an overdraft turns the race into an immediate failure.

quiz.q: Peak traffic is 3,000 transfers a second, and the journal write takes 4 ms. The disk allows 10 writes at once. What should the ledger pool's thread count be?
options: 12, from Little's law
10: the journal's limit is lower than what Little's law asks for
As many as the machine has cores
quiz.why: Little's law asks for 3,000 x 0.004 = 12, but the journal takes only 10 writes at once, so the 11th and 12th threads would only queue inside it. Size from the scarce resource: 10 threads give at most 10 / 0.004 = 2,500 transfers a second, and the counting rejection handles the rest.

quiz.q: Which rejection policy can silently lose a transfer that a customer was told was accepted?
options: A counting policy that throws
`CallerRunsPolicy`
`AbortPolicy`
`DiscardOldestPolicy`
quiz.why: `DiscardOldestPolicy` drops the oldest queued task, which a caller already holds a future for, and that future never completes. A throwing policy turns the new transfer away before anyone is told it was accepted, and `CallerRunsPolicy` runs it on the thread that submitted it.

quiz.q: A balances page adds up the accounts one at a time, locking each account while it reads it. Transfers keep running. What can it show?
options: Always the exact total, because every read holds a lock
A total that is too high or too low, because a transfer can run between two reads
An exception, because two locks are taken
A total that is always too low
quiz.why: Money can move from an account not yet read to one already read (counted in neither) or the other way (counted twice). Only holding every lock at once, in the global order, gives one moment.

quiz.q: A thread dump shows every `ledger-` thread `WAITING (parking)` on a `FutureTask` inside your own `statement` method, and no deadlock report. What is wrong?
options: Tasks waiting for other tasks queued in the same bounded pool
A lock-order deadlock between two accounts
The journal is slow
The pool's threads are pinned
quiz.why: Threads parked on futures of their own pool, with tasks still queued, is pool-induced deadlock: cooks waiting for tickets behind them on the rail. There is no lock cycle, so the JVM's detector reports nothing. Do the work inline, chain the next step instead of waiting, or use a separate pool.

quiz.q: Which design caps what the safety service sees when 10,000 requests run on virtual threads?
options: A fixed pool of 20 virtual threads for whole requests
A `Semaphore(20)` created in each request handler
`newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` on its own
One `Semaphore(20)` field on the safety client, shared by every request
quiz.why: One shared semaphore limits only the safety call. A pool of virtual threads caps the whole request, the daily-limit check and the ledger wait included. A semaphore per handler limits nothing, and the per-task executor has no limit at all.

quiz.q: On a bad day, each safety call takes 2 s. The request stops waiting at its 300 ms deadline but never cancels the call, and it uses a shared executor. What happens to the bulkhead?
options: Nothing: every request answers in 300 ms
It grows to fit the extra calls
Its permits stay held by abandoned calls for 2 s each, so most new requests can't get one
The calls are interrupted automatically
quiz.why: A timeout ends the wait, not the work. Each abandoned call keeps its permit until the safety service answers. Cancel the call at the deadline, so its `finally` gives the permit back to the next request.

quiz.q: The ledger must run on JDK 21 and serve virtual threads. Why are the account locks `ReentrantLock`s?
options: On JDK 21, a virtual thread waiting to enter, or waiting inside, `synchronized` pins its carrier; `ReentrantLock` lets it step off
`synchronized` doesn't make writes visible to other threads
`ReentrantLock` makes the critical section faster
Kotlin can't use `synchronized`
quiz.why: JDK 24 (JEP 491) removed that pinning, but on JDK 21 to 23 a waiting `synchronized` block holds the carrier, like a waiter holding a hot pan. `ReentrantLock` has always let a waiting virtual thread step off. Either way, nothing slow belongs inside an account lock.

quiz.q: `jcmd <pid> Thread.print` on the server during the safety service's bad day shows no request threads at all. Where are they?
options: They have all finished
They are inside the carriers, under the name `ForkJoinPool-1-worker-N`
The garbage collector removed them
They are waiting virtual threads, which `Thread.print` doesn't list; `Thread.dump_to_file -format=json` does
quiz.why: A waiting virtual thread is a stack on the heap, not an operating-system thread. `Thread.print` lists platform threads (plus virtual threads on a carrier, from JDK 24). The JSON dump lists every thread, grouped by the container that started it.
